title: Mechatronics — Software & Embedded Control
goal: The firmware/ side of the vault roadmap: sensor buses (I2C/SPI register maps), noise & FFT, complementary fusion, bare-metal STM32 registers, real-time determinism, FreeRTOS, PID, state-space, FOC, homing state machines, CAN, and SIL/V-model verification. Feeds Phase 2 milestones and QDD firmware in Phase 3. Prerequisites taught in sibling trees (circuits in mech-electronics, statics/dynamics in the spine and mech-mechanical, safety envelope in mech-project-safety) are referenced in claims, not edges.

sensor-bus.claim: A sensor on a bus is a tiny computer you interrogate: I2C uses an address plus a register map (write config, read data); SPI uses chip-select and shift registers; UART is asynchronous bytes. The first read is WHO_AM_I — verify identity before trusting any number. All three carry bytes; the difference is wires and handshake.
sensor-bus.probe: You plug in a new IMU. What is the first thing you read and why? Then: when would you pick SPI over I2C, and what does 'register map' mean physically?
rubric: WHO_AM_I identity register first — confirm you're talking to the right chip
SPI over I2C when speed/streaming matters (and CS selection when many devices)
register map = memory-mapped configuration and data on the device, written/read over the bus
sensor-bus.transfer_probe: A hotel: front desk routes requests by room number plus request type, walkie-talkies use channels, shouting across the lobby reaches everyone. Map I2C addressing, register maps, SPI chip-select, and the WHO_AM_I first-read onto checking in a guest — what do you verify before trusting the minibar bill?

noise-fft.claim: Noise is physical and structured, not 'bad signal': measurement noise has a frequency spectrum. The FFT is a diagnostic, not a filter — it tells you which frequencies carry your signal and which carry noise. Aliasing means high-frequency noise masquerades as low-frequency signal; you must filter BEFORE sampling, because after sampling it is permanent. ADC resolution is not accuracy: a 12-bit converter has 4096 steps, but noise, nonlinearity, and bandwidth cut the effective number of bits (ENOB) below the nameplate — resolution is the step size, accuracy is how close to truth.
noise-fft.probe: Your encoder reads jitter at 1 Hz that shouldn't exist. Give the two possible sources and how the FFT distinguishes them. Then explain why a digital filter on sampled data cannot fix aliasing that already happened. Finally: your ADC is 12-bit — what is the difference between resolution and accuracy, and why might the effective number of bits be less than 12?
rubric: either real 1 Hz mechanical/electrical content, or high-frequency content aliased down to 1 Hz
FFT of the raw signal + physical plausibility check (does 1 Hz exist anywhere in the plant?)
aliasing explained: content above Nyquist folds down; sampling cannot distinguish it
anti-alias filter must be analog, before the ADC
resolution = step size (12-bit → 4096 steps); accuracy = closeness to truth — noise/nonlinearity/bandwidth cut ENOB below 12

viz.hint: A time-domain squiggle whose spectrum you can flip open; drag a 500 Hz tone below the sampling rate and watch it fold back into view at 1 Hz. Caption: 'sampling is a photograph — motion in between is invented.'

noise-fft.transfer_probe: In a noisy cafe you try to follow one conversation through espresso-machine hiss and fridge hum. Map spectrum, FFT-as-diagnostic, why you cannot un-hear a misheard word (aliasing analogue), and resolution vs accuracy onto your hearing.

sensor-fusion.claim: Complementary fusion: the gyro is smooth but drifts (integrating it wanders); the accelerometer is noisy but absolute (gravity anchors it). The complementary filter trusts the gyro short-term and the accel long-term: angle = α·(angle + ω·dt) + (1−α)·accel_angle. Calibrate the gyro bias first — it is the leak in the filter. Calibration and filtering are different jobs: calibration removes systematic error (offset, scale factor, alignment, temperature drift); filtering removes random noise — neither substitutes for the other.
sensor-fusion.probe: Why can't you just use the accelerometer alone, or just integrate the gyro alone? Write the complementary filter update line, say what α does, and name the one thing you must calibrate first. Then: a temperature shift drifts your angle reading — is that a calibration problem or a filtering problem, and what do you do about it?
rubric: accel: noisy/gravity-ambiguous under linear acceleration; gyro: bias causes unbounded drift
filter equation with α blending gyro-incremented and accel-derived angle
α sets the crossover: high α = trust gyro, low α = trust accel
gyro bias calibration first
calibration vs filtering: temperature drift is systematic — calibrate (bias/scale/temp compensation); random noise is filtered; they are complementary

bare-metal-stm32.claim: Bare-metal STM32 means registers, not libraries: RCC gates clocks; GPIOx_MODER sets pin mode; TIM generates PWM and counts encoder edges; SPI/I2C/USART are shift registers with status flags. The pattern is always the same: enable clock → configure pin function → configure peripheral → poll or interrupt on flag → read/write the data register. 'Volatile' marks memory the hardware changes.
bare-metal-stm32.probe: Write the four-step sequence to make a timer toggle a GPIO pin on an STM32 (no HAL): name the register families in order and what each does. Then explain why the data register must be declared volatile.
rubric: RCC clock enable first (peripheral is dead without it)
GPIO MODER configured to alternate function
TIM configured: prescaler, auto-reload, PWM channel on
volatile: compiler must not cache a value the hardware changes
bare-metal-stm32.transfer_probe: An espresso machine: mains switch gates everything, the grind dial sets the mode, the brew button plus ready-light is a flag poll, the shot is the data register. Map enable-clock, configure-function, flag-poll, read-data — plus what 'volatile' would mean for the water-level sensor — onto pulling a shot.

practice.problem_frame: Given a peripheral task (PWM, encoder count, UART echo) and a pin, write the register-level initialization sequence.
practice.discriminates_from: Copying a HAL call without knowing the clock → function → peripheral → flag ordering.
practice.verify: Trace each register against the reference manual; the peripheral must be clocked before any other write takes effect.
error_bank: configuring the peripheral before enabling its clock
forgetting the MODER switch to alternate function
missing volatile or polling the wrong flag bit

realtime-determinism.claim: Hard real-time means the deadline is part of correctness: a 1 kHz motor-control loop that occasionally misses a tick is wrong, even if it's usually on time. Determinism comes from bounding worst-case time: no dynamic allocation in the loop, no blocking waits, ISRs do the minimum, and a timer — never a 'delay' — drives the rhythm.
realtime-determinism.probe: Your control loop calls malloc, reads a file, and prints to UART. Rank which ones break hard real-time and why. Then describe the correct skeleton: what wakes the loop, what exactly must stay constant tick to tick, what belongs in the ISR versus the main loop — and what discipline bounds the worst case?
rubric: malloc and file I/O break it (unbounded worst-case time); UART print blocks unless DMA/queue
timer-driven wake at fixed period — no delay()-based pacing
ISR: minimum work, copy data, set flag; main loop: control math
WCET analysis is the discipline

viz.hint: A 1 kHz tick train; each loop iteration is a colored block you can drag in (malloc = red, print = amber, pure math = green). Jitter shows as the green blocks sliding off the tick marks.

realtime-determinism.transfer_probe: A kitchen must fire a plate every 5 minutes during service — a perfect plate that arrives late is wrong. Map no-allocation-in-the-loop, ISR-minimum, and timer-driven rhythm onto the pass: what is the kitchen's malloc, its ISR, its timer?

freertos.claim: FreeRTOS is preemptive multitasking with priorities: the highest-priority ready task runs; tasks communicate through queues and mutexes; a watchdog turns a hang into a reset; priority inversion is the classic bug, solved by priority inheritance. But the control task still runs on a timer at 1 kHz — the RTOS organizes, the clock commands.
freertos.probe: Three tasks: control (1 kHz), telemetry (10 Hz), LCD (1 Hz). Assign priorities and justify. Then describe priority inversion with a mutex and how inheritance fixes it. On what must the control task never block?
rubric: control highest, telemetry mid, LCD lowest — or control pinned by the timer ISR
inversion: low-priority task holds a mutex the high-priority task wants, so a mid-priority task starves the high one
inheritance: the mutex holder inherits the waiter's priority until release
control task: never blocks on a queue the slower tasks produce

pid-control.claim: PID is a three-voice plan for error: P scales the correction to the present error, I integrates past error to kill steady-state offset (and must be clamped — windup), D anticipates by looking at the error's slope (and amplifies noise). Tune physics-first: compute gains from the plant model, then adjust one voice at a time.
pid-control.probe: A cart sits 10 cm off target, not moving. Which term fixes the offset and why? The D term makes the loop jitter — what is happening and what is the fix? Give the one-line job of each of the three terms. In what order do you tune, starting from what?
rubric: I kills steady-state offset (P alone leaves a residual; D is zero because nothing is changing)
D amplifies sensor noise (error slope is mostly noise) — filter the derivative or reduce D
P = present error, I = past accumulation (clamp it — windup), D = future slope
tuning order: physics estimate, then one term at a time

viz.hint: A cart-and-track with three sliders (Kp, Ki, Kd): drag each term live, watch overshoot/offset/oscillation emerge; a windup meter shows when the integrator saturates.

pid-control.transfer_probe: Your shower runs cold so you crank it hot (overshoot), keep cranking while waiting (worse overshoot), then flinch at every flicker (jitter). Map P, I with windup, and D with noise onto the shower — what is the physics-first fix in each case?

practice.problem_frame: Given a plant model or step response, choose P/I/D gains to meet response targets and diagnose a behavior (offset, overshoot, jitter).
practice.discriminates_from: Blind gain-stabbing; treating D as a fix for steady-state error.
practice.verify: Simulate the tuned loop before hardware; check no term is saturated (windup clamp engaged).
error_bank: using I for a system that has no offset problem (invites oscillation)
raising D until it oscillates from noise amplification
integrator windup on a saturated actuator

state-space.claim: State-space is dynamics as a vector ODE: M(q)q̈ + C(q,q̇)q̇ + g(q) = τ — the inertia matrix, Coriolis/centrifugal terms, and gravity. The arm's response depends on configuration: inertia changes as it extends. Linearize about an operating point to get A, B, then LQR gives provably stable feedback gains. The equations are the model; the sim is where you meet it.
state-space.probe: Write the rigid-arm equation in standard form and name each term physically. Why can't one fixed set of gains serve the arm both tucked and fully extended? What does linearization sacrifice — and once linearized, what design method gives the feedback gains?
rubric: M(q)q̈ + C(q,q̇)q̇ + g(q) = τ with each term identified
configuration-dependent inertia — gains tuned for one pose may destabilize another
linearize about an operating point → A, B; LQR on the linear model
linearization is valid only near the operating point

viz.hint: A 2-link arm with a small 'linearization radius' disc that travels with the pose; outside the disc the model drifts from truth. Caption: 'the equations don't lie — your operating point does.'

state-space.transfer_probe: A delivery bike handles differently empty versus loaded with 30 kg over the rear wheel — one fixed riding style fails both. Map configuration-dependent inertia and what linearization sacrifices onto the bike: what is your A-matrix linearized around, and when does it stop describing the ride?

foc-loop.claim: FOC is a current servo in a rotating frame: measure two phase currents, transform to the rotor's frame (Clarke → Park, needing the electrical angle), regulate Id → 0 and Iq → torque in DC-like coordinates, then inverse-transform to phase voltages. All the magic is the coordinate transform; the hard-won calibration is the encoder's electrical offset.
foc-loop.probe: Why does FOC regulate currents in a rotating frame instead of the phase frame directly? Name the two transforms and the angle they need. What does Id = 0 mean physically? What single calibration is the usual failure point?
rubric: rotating frame turns sinusoids into DC, so a PI loop works
Clarke (3-phase → 2-axis) then Park (rotating → rotor frame) with electrical angle
Id = 0: no wasted field component; Iq is the torque-producing current
electrical offset calibration is the failure point

homing-statemachines.claim: Homing is a two-pass state machine: move to the switch, back off, then approach slowly — the second pass defeats bounce and direction bias. Limit switches fail safe as normally-closed: a broken wire reads as tripped. Every arm is a state machine — IDLE → HOMING → READY → RUNNING → FAULT — and FAULT latches until an explicit reset.
homing-statemachines.probe: Why two passes instead of one? Why normally-closed switches? Draw the arm's state machine and say what happens when a joint exceeds its limit during RUNNING.
rubric: two-pass: fast approach, back off, slow approach — bounce and direction-bias defeated
normally-closed fails safe: open wire = tripped, not 'no switch'
state machine correct with FAULT as a latching state
limit violation during RUNNING → enter FAULT, require explicit recovery

can-messaging.claim: CAN is a multi-master differential serial bus for actuators: messages carry an ID whose priority IS the arbitration (lower ID wins), nodes have no addresses — they filter by ID; termination resistors at both ends are mandatory. A CAN frame is either delivered or it is garbage. Message design — periodic vs event, the ID map — is architecture, not wiring.
can-messaging.probe: Two nodes transmit at once — how does CAN decide? Why is 120 Ω termination at both ends non-negotiable? Design the arm's message map: which message deserves the lowest ID and why?
rubric: arbitration by ID: the dominant (lower) ID wins bit-by-bit
termination: impedance match at both ends prevents reflections; two 120 Ω = 60 Ω bus
nodes filter by ID — no addresses
lowest ID for safety/E-stop and control — highest priority, lowest latency

v-model-sil.claim: The V-model gates hardware with simulation: SIL runs the real control code against a simulated plant — actuator limits, friction, and noise in the loop — so first power-on is a confirmation, not a discovery. HIL connects the real controller to the simulated plant. Anything you can crash in simulation costs nothing; the same crash on hardware costs a build.
v-model-sil.probe: Before applying power to the QDD for the first time, you run SIL. Name three things SIL must include to be meaningful and one thing it fundamentally cannot verify.
rubric: actuator limits (saturation, current cap) in the plant model
friction, inertia, and sensor noise modeled
the exact controller code that will run on hardware
cannot verify: wiring, current sensing reality, EMI, power integrity — real-electronics issues

capstone.claim: You can USE Mechatronics — Software & Embedded Control in your own work, not just explain it.
capstone.probe: Build the thing. In your real repo, your real notes, your real argument — produce something that only works if you actually understand Mechatronics — Software & Embedded Control. Your stated goal: The firmware/ side of the vault roadmap: sensor buses (I2C/SPI register maps), noise & FFT, complementary fusion, bare-metal STM32 registers, real-time determinism, FreeRTOS, PID, state-space, FOC, homing state machines, CAN, and SIL/V-model verification. Feeds Phase 2 milestones and QDD firmware in Phase 3. Prerequisites taught in sibling trees (circuits in mech-electronics, statics/dynamics in the spine and mech-mechanical, safety envelope in mech-project-safety) are referenced in claims, not edges.. Ship it, then explain which concept made which decision.
rubric: the artifact exists and works (or the argument stands on its own)
names at least two concepts from this topic that DECIDED something in it
identifies where the model broke down or needed more than the topic gave

toolchain-cmake-gdb.claim: Bare metal means owning the whole build: a CMakeLists written from scratch, a custom linker script plus startup flow you can narrate, OpenOCD + GDB breakpoints (not printf) as the debugger, a 1 kHz ISR verified against scope jitter, SPI modes (CPOL/CPHA, CS-as-GPIO) proven on the analyzer, UART framing with the baud divisor derived from the APB clock, and timer encoder mode at 4× with 16-bit overflow math (Δcount/Δt plus input filter) — commit known-good, diff when broken.
toolchain-cmake-gdb.probe: Fresh clone will not link: walk the bring-up from CMakeLists through linker, startup, and first GDB halt. Prove SPI mode/CS-as-GPIO and the UART divisor on hardware. Encoder at 8000 counts/rev on a 16-bit timer: revolutions before overflow, unwrap method, input-filter setting - and how is the ISR rate verified?
rubric: CMakeLists + linker + startup narrated; GDB halts at main via OpenOCD (debugger, not printf)
SPI mode/CS + UART divisor-from-clock proven on hardware, not assumed from example code
encoder 4× + overflow math (65535 ÷ 8000 ≈ 8 revs) with unwrap + input-filter setting; ISR rate verified on scope

viz.hint: Size it for a real rail, phase, or bus; the numbers decide, not the habit.

can-cpp-integrity.claim: A bus shared with a spinning arm is a contract, not a cable: static allocation only (no new/malloc, no exceptions, no RTTI), one CANObject base with concrete message types, bit-timing with documented sample point, versioned structs (endianness + heartbeat + timeout + safe default on stale), CRC plus sequence numbers, proven bus-off/overrun recovery, 1000 packets with zero drops, and -Wall -Wextra clean.
can-cpp-integrity.probe: A stale torque command arrives mid-move: what in your stack catches it, what safe state results, and which three proofs (build flags, packet test, fault test) show the reviewer?
rubric: static-only C++ (CANObject + 2 types, no heap/exceptions/RTTI) with -Wall -Wextra clean
version/heartbeat/timeout + CRC/sequence → stale command lands a defined safe default, not last-good
bus-off/overrun recovery demonstrated; 1000-packet zero-drop; bit-timing/sample-point documented

viz.hint: Size it for a real rail, phase, or bus; the numbers decide, not the habit.
